pages.summary: Images made larger or smaller, turned, cropped and moved.
body: `imresize` scales by a factor or to a size (NaN for one side keeps the aspect ratio), by `'bicubic'` interpolation unless another method is named; when shrinking, the kernel widens so that fine detail is averaged rather than lost. `imrotate` turns counterclockwise (by `'nearest'` unless `'bilinear'` or `'bicubic'`), the result large enough for all of it unless `'crop'`; quarter turns are exact. `imcrop` keeps the pixels whose centres lie in [xmin ymin width height]; `imtranslate` moves the image tx columns right and ty rows down, filling what is uncovered. Each keeps the image's class.

examples.title: A small image transformed

pages.summary: Images filtered by kernels: any kernel, the common ones, Gaussian and box filters, and integral images.
body: `imfilter` correlates an image with a kernel (or convolves with `'conv'`), its centre at floor((size(h) + 1)/2), the edge padded with zeros, a value, `'symmetric'`, `'replicate'` or `'circular'`; colour planes alike, the result in the image's class. `fspecial` makes kernels: average, disk, Gaussian, Laplacian, Laplacian of Gaussian, motion blur, Prewitt, Sobel and unsharp. `imgaussfilt` smooths by a Gaussian of standard deviation sigma (0.5), the edge replicated; `imboxfilt` by a box. `integralImage` gives the running sums from the corner, so that any rectangle's sum takes four lookups.

examples.title: Blurring and edges from kernels
Rectangle sums in four lookups

pages.summary: Each pixel the median, or another order statistic, of its neighbourhood.
body: `medfilt2` takes the median of each m-by-n neighbourhood (3-by-3), which removes salt-and-pepper noise and keeps edges; beyond the edge the image is zeros unless `'symmetric'`. `ordfilt2` takes the order-th smallest of the neighbours where a domain is true: the smallest is a minimum filter, the largest a maximum filter.

examples.title: Salt and pepper removed

pages.summary: Edges of a gray image, and its gradients.
body: `edge` gives a logical image of edges: by the Sobel (default), Prewitt or Roberts gradient above a threshold, the zero crossings of the Laplacian of Gaussian, or Canny's method (thin edges linked by two thresholds); without a threshold one is chosen, and the second output gives it. `imgradientxy` gives the gradients to the right and down (Sobel, Prewitt, central or intermediate differences); `imgradient` their magnitude and direction (degrees counterclockwise from the x axis, y up).

examples.title: Four methods on one shape

pages.summary: Contrast: the histogram, and intensities mapped to spread or match it.
body: `imhist` counts the pixels in n bins (256) over the class's range, and draws the histogram without outputs. `stretchlim` gives limits that leave out the darkest and brightest 1%; `imadjust` maps a range of intensities onto another (by default those limits onto [0 1]), with a gamma curve between. `histeq` maps the intensities through their cumulative distribution so that the histogram is spread flat; `adapthisteq` does it tile by tile, the histograms clipped so that noise is not amplified (CLAHE), blending the tiles' mappings. `imhistmatch` maps an image so that its histogram is like another's.

examples.title: A dull image stretched and equalized

pages.summary: Thresholds by Otsu's method, images split by them, and the negative.
body: `graythresh` gives the level (0 to 1) that best separates the pixels into two classes, the variance between them largest; `otsuthresh` does the same for a histogram; `multithresh` finds several thresholds at once (exactly, by dynamic programming), and `imquantize` splits values into classes by them. `imbinarize` makes a gray image logical at Otsu's level (or one given); `im2bw` is the older form, at 0.5 unless given. `imcomplement` gives the negative.
syntax: Of a histogram, and how well it separates.
